nameStory: This ruffle lichen gets its genus name from the way its edges curl and ripple like fabric ruffles on a fancy dress. The species name 'diffractaicum' refers to how light seems to bend and scatter across its complex, folded surface - like light diffracting through a prism.
description: This is a medium-sized foliose lichen that grows flat against tree bark like a leafy medallion. Its gray-green body forms irregular patches up to 4-6 inches across, with distinctive wavy, ruffled edges that curl upward from the surface. The upper surface has a somewhat powdery appearance when dry, and the whole lichen looks like someone carefully arranged crinkled tissue paper on the bark.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface feels slightly rough and has a distinctly powdery or frosted appearance, especially when dry - like someone dusted it with fine flour

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms leafy, flat patches against bark with characteristically wavy, ruffled edges that curl up and away from the surface

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to bluish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet from rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on the bark of hardwood trees, particularly favoring oak, maple, and ash trees

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Produces powdery granules called soredia along the edges and surface that feel gritty when rubbed gently with a finger

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches typically reach 3-6 inches across, though multiple patches may grow together to cover larger areas of bark

habitat: Found on the bark of mature hardwood trees in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England. Prefers somewhat sheltered locations with moderate humidity, often on the north-facing sides of trees or in partially shaded woodland areas. Most commonly spotted on oaks, maples, and ash trees in established forests rather than young or disturbed woodlands.

seasonality.spring: Appears fresh and vibrant green after spring rains, making it easier to spot against darker bark. The powdery surface texture is most noticeable when it dries out between rain showers.
seasonality.summer: May look duller and grayer during dry spells, but morning dew often reveals its true green colors. Growth is most active during humid summer conditions.
seasonality.fall: Remains visible as leaves drop, actually becoming more obvious on bare branches. Colors may appear more muted but the distinctive ruffled texture remains clear.
seasonality.winter: Stays present and identifiable year-round, though it may look flatter against the bark. Snow and ice can temporarily obscure it but won't damage the lichen.

funFact: This lichen can actually change its metabolism based on which partner is dominant - sometimes the fungus takes the lead, other times the algae calls the shots, making it like a tiny organism with multiple personalities that switch depending on conditions.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with perforated ruffle lichen, but that species has distinctive holes or perforations in its surface that look like tiny windows - this species lacks those telltale holes and has a more uniformly powdery surface instead.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, this species is extremely rare in our region and represents the northern edge of its range. Finding one would be a significant discovery worth reporting to local naturalist groups or lichen societies.
compareHints: Unlike perforated ruffle lichen which has obvious holes, or powdered ruffle lichen which has coarser granules, this species has a fine, evenly distributed powdery coating. It differs from black stone flower by lacking the distinctive black lower surface, and from salted ruffle lichen by having finer, less chunky reproductive structures along its edges.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike perforated ruffle lichen which has distinctive holes, powdered ruffle lichen has a continuous surface covered in soredia.
Unlike its powdered ruffle lichen cousin which has a dusty, powdery surface, perforated ruffle lichen has a smooth surface and those unmistakable perforated fruiting bodies.
Salted ruffle lichen stands out from its ruffle lichen relatives by those distinctive white, salt-like granules scattered across its surface.

Unlike its relatives the Perforated Ruffle Lichen (which has distinctive holes) or the Powdered Ruffle Lichen (which has a dusty, powdery surface), Black Sheet Lichen has a smooth, unperforated surface.
Among its ruffle lichen relatives, Black Stone Flower stands out with its prominent soralia (powdery patches) near the lobe edges and distinctive black cilia.

Compared to its Parmotrema relatives, Lacy Powdered-ruffle has the most delicate and intricate lobe margins - while Powdered Ruffle Lichen has broader, less ornate edges and Perforated Ruffle Lichen has distinctive holes.
